description:
The Step Jack is a low-impact plyometric-style move that provides cardiovascular benefits without the joint stress of jumping. It works the entire body, specifically targeting the legs, core, and shoulders. This move is ideal for beginners, individuals with joint sensitivities, or as a dynamic warm-up to gradually elevate the heart rate.
Notes (Instructions):
1. ​Stand upright with your feet together and arms at your sides.
2. ​Step your right foot out to the side while simultaneously swinging both arms up above your head.
3. Bring your right foot back to the center and lower your arms.
4. ​Immediately repeat the movement, stepping out with your left foot.
5. ​Continue alternating sides at a steady, rhythmic pace.
name: Step Jack

description:
​A tempo-based squat that uses controlled movement to increase muscle tension and improve lower-body stability.
1. ​Lower: Descend slowly for 3 seconds.
2. ​Pause: Hold at the bottom for 1 second.
3. ​Stand: Return to the starting position at a normal pace.
4. Form: Keep your chest up and weight in your heels.
name: Slow Squat

description:
​A push-up variation with a wider hand placement to increase the emphasis on the outer chest muscles and shoulders.
1. ​Setup: Place hands wider than shoulder-width apart on the floor.
2. Lower: Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your core tight.
3. ​Push: Drive through your palms to return to the start position.
4. ​Form: Don't let your lower back sag; keep a straight line from head to heels.
name: Wide Push-Up

description:
A low-impact cardio and mobility exercise that strengthens the hip flexors and improves balance.
1. ​Movement: Stand tall and lift one knee toward your chest as high as comfortable.
2. ​Arms: Swing the opposite arm forward as you lift your knee, similar to a walking motion.
3. ​Core: Keep your abs engaged to maintain an upright posture.
4. ​Pace: Perform the movement with control, alternating legs rhythmically.
name: Marching High Knees

description:
- Begin in a half kneeling position with the
leg away from the wall stabilized against the wall
with a ball.
- With both hands directly in front of
you, rotate one arm open attempting to reach
the wall behind you.
- Exhale as you rotate, inhale
as you return to neutral and repeat.
name: 1/2 Kneeling Thoracic Rotation

description: slow controlled seated forward exercise with dumbbells
name: lento avanti seduto

description: Press the dumbbell vertically overhead in a controlled motion until your arm is fully extended, without locking the elbow. Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position at shoulder height.
name: Single-arm dumbbell shoulder press

description:
Single-arm cable pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise that targets the triceps brachii. By working one arm at a time, it helps correct strength imbalances between sides while also engaging the core for stability.
Starting position:
Stand facing the cable machine with your feet shoulder-width apart. Attach a single handle to the high pulley. Grab the handle with one hand using an overhand grip (pronated), with your elbow bent at approximately 90° and tucked close to your body. Keep your core braced and your back straight.
Execution:
Push the handle downward in a controlled motion by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended. Hold the contraction for 1 second at the bottom, then slowly return to the starting position.
name: Single-arm cable pushdown

description:
A compound exercise combining elements of a sumo deadlift and a high pull. It targets the posterior chain, particularly the glutes, hamstrings, and upper back. The sumo stance increases hip engagement, while the high pull adds an explosive element, promoting power development.
- Stand upright overtop of a kettlebell with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart angled out slightly.
- Maintain a braced core and neutral spine throughout the exercise.
- Hinge your hips backward and extend your arms to grab ahold the kettlebell with a double overhand grip.
- With you lower legs nearly vertical to the ground, extend your hips to raise the kettlebell with your elbows high keeping it close to your body.
- Once the kettlebell has reached shoulder height, lower back to the starting position.
name: Kettlebell sumo high pull

description: Close grip front facing Pull down, while focusing on Biceps, Increases activation of biceps over the whole range, Avoid activating Lats.
name: Mentzer Pulldown

description: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grab the single handle with a neutral grip. Keep your torso stable, your chest lifted, and your shoulder blades slightly retracted. Start with your arm fully extended overhead, then pull the handle down toward your upper chest following a controlled, slightly diagonal path. Focus on engaging the latissimus dorsi while keeping the shoulder depressed and avoiding any torso rotation. Slowly return to the starting position, maintaining full control throughout the movement.
name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown

description:
Stand on one leg and lean your upper body slightly forward while keeping your back straight. Extend the free leg behind you so that your torso and leg form roughly one line. Slowly open your hip to the side by rotating your pelvis and upper body in a controlled way. Then close the hip again and return to the starting position.
The movement should mainly come from the hip. Keep your standing foot stable and avoid letting your knee collapse inward.
name: Hip Airplane

description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your knees stacked on top of each other. Keep your feet together at first, then keep your knees touching while lifting your top foot upward. Slowly lower the foot back down with control.
Move only through the hip and avoid rolling your pelvis backward. The movement should be small, controlled, and focused on hip rotation.
name: Reverse Clamshell

description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your legs stacked. Lift your top knee into a clamshell position and keep the leg elevated throughout the movement. From there, alternate between opening the knee upward and lifting the foot upward, moving through hip external and internal rotation.
Keep the movement slow and controlled. Do not let the top leg rest on the bottom leg between repetitions.
name: Clamshell to Reverse Clamshell

description:
This is a variation of the flat bench press designed to emphasize the clavicular head of the pectoralis major (the upper portion). By tilting the torso, the angle of the push changes, shifting more tension to the upper chest and shoulders, which helps achieve a more aesthetic, balanced, and three-dimensional development of the torso.
1.
Starting Position: Grip a bar with an overhand grip (palms facing up) at a width similar to your shoulders.
2.
Position on the Bench: Kneel in front of a flat bench and rest the backs of your forearms on it. Your wrists and hands should extend slightly beyond the edge of the bench to allow for a full range of motion.
3.
Eccentric Phase (Lowering): Lower the bar in a controlled manner by extending your wrists toward the floor. At the bottom of the movement, slightly spread your fingers to let the bar roll down a bit, maximizing the stretch.
4.
Concentric Phase (Lift): First, close your fingers to secure the bar, then flex your wrists upward explosively but in a controlled manner, bringing the bar as high as possible. Strongly contract your forearms at the top position for one second.
5.
Form: Keep your forearms firmly pressed against the bench throughout the exercise; only your wrists and fingers should move.
name: Curl De Muñeca Con Barra

description: The YTW exercise for scapular retraction is designed to strengthen the inter-scapular muscles between your shoulder blades, to help retract or pull your shoulders back, helping to maintain proper upright posture.
name: YTW Raises

description: Kneel on a glute-ham developer or have a partner hold your ankles. Keeping hips straight, lower your torso toward the floor under control, then curl back up by contracting the hamstrings and glutes.
name: Glute-Ham Raise

description: Swim freestyle at a relaxed, steady pace without stopping — think conversation pace, not racing. Focus on smooth, even strokes rather than speed or breathing technique; this is just to get your body moving and your heart rate up.
name: Easy Continuous Swim (Freestyle)

description: Hold a kickboard with both hands, arms extended in front of you, face in the water (lift head forward to breathe when needed). Kick from your hips, not your knees, keeping your legs mostly straight with a slight bend and a steady, compact flutter kick. This builds leg endurance and keeps your body horizontal without needing to worry about your arms.
name: Kick with Board

description: Stand in chest-deep water. Take a breath, submerge your face fully, and exhale slowly and completely through your nose and/or mouth the whole time you're underwater — a gentle humming sound can help keep the exhale steady and controlled. Once you're empty of air, lift your head, take a fresh breath, and go back under. Repeat continuously. The goal is training your body that all your exhaling happens underwater, so all you need to do at the surface is inhale.
name: Bobbing Exhale Drill

description: Hold the pool wall or edge with one hand, body horizontal at the surface, legs kicking gently behind you. Keep your face in the water, exhaling continuously, then rotate your head to the side — not lifting it up — so one goggle stays in the water while the other clears the surface. Take a quick breath, then rotate your face back down to neutral. This isolates the head-rotation motion without any arm strokes to think about.
name: Wall-Hold Rotation

description: Push off the wall on your side (not flat on your stomach), one arm extended forward holding the board or just extended, kicking continuously. Keep your head in a neutral position looking at the bottom of the pool, and when you need air, rotate your head sideways (one ear stays in the water, other faces up) to breathe, then rotate back to neutral. Swim a length like this, then repeat on the other side. This teaches the exact head position and rotation you'll use once full stroke breathing comes in.
name: Side-Kick Breathing (Kickboard)

description: Push off, swim a few strokes, and every breath roll fully onto your back for 2-3 breaths, then roll back into freestyle. This teaches you to rotate your body as a unit rather than just turning your head, and helps remove the fear of not having your face in the water.
name: Stroke-and-Roll Drill

description: Same motion as the Bobbing Exhale Drill, but done in slightly deeper water (so you're not touching the bottom) and at a slower, more relaxed pace — think of it as a recovery/reset exercise rather than a hard drill. Use it between harder drills to reset your breathing rhythm and calm down if you're feeling rushed or out of sync.
name: Recovery Bobbing

description: Swim at an easy, unhurried pace — freestyle, backstroke, or just floating/gliding — with zero focus on technique or drills. The only goal here is to let your heart rate come down gradually and your muscles relax before you get out of the pool.
name: Cool-Down Swim

aliases: Pelvic Tilt Drill / Supine Pelvic Tilt
description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Flatten your lower back against the floor by tilting your pelvis posteriorly, engaging your abs and glutes. Hold 5 seconds, release. This retrains pelvic positioning to counter anterior pelvic tilt.
name: Posterior Pelvic Tilt

description: This is an end range strengthening exercise for the knee extensors. Start by looping a band around the back of one knee and anchoring the other end to a stable surface in front of you. Stand in a split stance with the banded knee bent and placed as the front leg. Straighten the knee to pull against the bands resistance and maintain a contraction in your quadriceps for up to 5 seconds before releasing.
name: Band Terminal Knee extension

description:
1. Stand facing a wall. Place your forearms vertically against the wall so your elbows and wrists are both touching it.
2. Point your arms slightly outwards from "straight up".
3. Protract your shoulders hard, then slide your forearms up the wall until your elbows are about level with your chin.
4. Slide your forearms back down the wall. Repeat as necessary.
name: Serratus Wall Slide Stretch

description:
1. Stand facing away from a bench, couch or similar-height object.
2. Extend one leg backwards, resting your foot "laces-down" on the edge of the bench.
3. Lower yourself until your rear knee is on the floor and you are in a lunge position, with your torso hanging forwards slightly.
4. Brace your core, tense your rear glute, and straighten up your torso to vertical, under control. Relax and repeat.
Repeat for the other leg, too.
name: Couch Stretch

description:
1. Hold the resistance band (or any other rope-like object, the elasticity is not necessary) above your head, between your hands, with your arms straight. Pull it taught to engage your lats.
2. Step forwards into a lunge, dropping until your knee is almost touching the floor.
3. Slowly and controlledly pulse your body up and down by about an inch. Repeat for required reps.
4. Repeat for other leg.
name: Long Lunge Pulse Stretch

description:
1. Start kneeling.
2. Extend one leg out forwards, fully straightened. Follow with your hips so your back leg begins to unfold.
3. Carefully lower yourself into the stretch. Do not go beyond your limit.
4. Hold for the required time.
name: Front Split Stretch

description:
1. Drop into a squat.
2. Hold one ankle with the opposite hand.
3. Fold your other arm to your chest.
4. Staying in the squat and keeping hold of your ankle, twist to turn your chest-hand back/outwards until your elbow is pointing at the sky.
5. Return to the neutral squatting position with your hand on your chest. Repeat movement as required.
Repeat on both sides.
name: Squat Sky Reach Stretch

description:
Explosive Push-Ups
Start in a standard push-up position, lower your chest, then explosively push off the ground so your hands leave the floor. Land softly and immediately repeat.
name: Explosive Push-Ups

description:
Russian Push-Ups
Start in a standard push-up position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Lower your chest toward the floor, then shift your body forward while keeping your chest close to the ground. Extend your arms to return to the starting position, then reverse the movement smoothly. Keep your core tight and maintain controlled movement throughout the exercise.
name: Russian Push Ups

description: ​A calisthenics static balance skill where the entire body is held straight and parallel to the ground, supported by tucking the elbows firmly into the abdomen or pelvic bones.
name: elbow lever

description: A straight-arm calisthenics static hold where you assume a plank position and lean the shoulders as far forward as possible past the wrists with protracted scapulae and a hollow body.
name: Planche Lean Hold

description: An isometric leg extension is a strengthening exercise where you contract your quadriceps muscles against an immovable resistance without changing the length of the muscle or moving your knee joint.
name: Leg Extension Isometric

description: A bench press isometric hold is a static strength exercise where you pause and hold a barbell or dumbbells either at your chest, mid-press, or at lockout without moving for a set time
name: Bench Press Isometric

description: An isometric overhead press involves holding a weight statically overhead or pushing against an immovable object at a specific point in the press without moving the joint.
name: Overhead Press Isometric

description: An isometric lateral raise is a shoulder exercise where you hold your arms out to the sides at waist height for a set amount of time instead of moving up and down
name: Lateral Raise Isometric

description: An isometric preacher curl is a static strength exercise where you hold a fixed position on a preacher pad or and inclined bench under tension without moving the joint.
name: Preacher Curl Isometric

description: An isometric Lat pulldown is a strength-building exercise where you pull the bar down to your chest and hold the contracted position at the bottom without moving your limbs for a set number of seconds
name: Lat Pulldown Isometric

description: A single-arm isometric or isolated triceps pushdown is an isolation cable exercise where you pin your upper arm against your torso, hinge at the hips, and extend the elbow to achieve a peak contraction in the triceps muscle.
name: Triceps Pushdown Isometric

description: Bag workout for boxing skill development and cardio improvement
name: Boxing

description: Wrist circles is warm-up exercise, where you rotate your wrists in a circular motion. They improve mobility and are recommended before exercises such as pull ups, hand stands and other exercises that put pressure on your wrists.
name: Wrist circles

description: Controlled treadmill walking performed backward, at a slow and steady speed. A slight incline of about 2 to 3 percent can be added if tolerated.
name: Retro Treadmill Walking

description:
Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit upright in a chair. Locate the pelvic floor muscles: they are the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or to hold back gas. Keep your abdomen, glutes and thighs relaxed and breathe normally throughout.
Tighten the pelvic floor muscles and lift them gently upwards and inwards. Hold the contraction for a few seconds, then release completely and rest for at least as long as you held. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
The exercise can be varied by holding longer with a light contraction (endurance) or by performing quick, short contractions with a full relaxation in between.
name: Kegel Exercise

description:
Stand in a split stance with one foot about a stride in front of the other, and hold on to a stable support such as a rack, a wall or the back of a chair.
Lower your hips straight down by bending both knees until the back knee almost touches the floor. Keep your upper body upright and the front heel on the floor, then push through the front foot back up. Use the support only for balance, not to pull yourself up. Complete all repetitions, then switch sides.
name: Supported Split Squat

description: Controlled breathing drill performed in a 90/90 position to encourage rib, abdominal, and pelvic coordination.
name: 90/90 Breathing

description:
Sit on the floor with one leg bent at 90 degrees in front of you and the other leg bent at 90 degrees out to the side, so that the rear shin is parallel to the front shin. Keep your torso upright and, if possible, your hands off the floor.
Rotate both knees over to the other side so that the legs swap positions and you arrive in the same 90/90 position facing the opposite way. Move slowly and under control, keeping the feet in contact with the floor, and alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions.
Mobility drill for internal and external rotation of the hips.
name: 90/90 Hip Switches

description:
Start on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips. Extend one leg straight out to the side with the foot flat on the floor and the toes pointing forward.
Keep your back flat and slowly push your hips back towards the heel of the kneeling leg until you feel a stretch along the inside of the extended leg. Pause briefly, then return to the starting position. Complete all repetitions on one side before switching legs.
Mobility exercise for the adductors and the hips.
name: Adductor Rock Backs

description:
Stand facing a bar, box or bench at roughly hip height and place the heel of one leg on it. Keep that leg straight with the toes pointing up, and keep the standing leg straight with both hips square to the support.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in the back of the elevated thigh. Hold the position while breathing calmly, then switch legs.
Stretch for the hamstrings. The height of the support controls the intensity: the higher the leg, the stronger the stretch.
name: Elevated Hamstring Stretch

description:
Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.
Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
- Improves Balance: Standing on one leg challenges your stability.
- Enhances Coordination: Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.
- Strengthens Core: The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.
How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
1. Positioning: Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.
2. Balance: Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.
3. Duration: Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.
Progression Tips
- Add Movement: Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.
- Close Your Eyes: This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.
- Use a Ball: Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.
This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.
name: Single-leg BOSU balance

description:
What Are Quad Sets?
Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.
How to Perform Quad Sets
Steps to Execute Quad Sets
1. Positioning: Sit or lie down with your legs straight.
2. Tightening: Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.
3. Holding: Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.
4. Releasing: Relax the muscle after the hold.
5. Repetitions: Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.
Tips for Effective Quad Sets
- Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.
- Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.
- It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.
Benefits of Quad Sets
- Restores Muscle Function: Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.
- Improves Stability: Enhances stability in the knee joint.
- Increases Range of Motion: Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.
Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.
name: Quad Sets

description:
Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps
Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.
Exercise Descriptions
Hip-Out Steps
- Movement: Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.
- Target Muscles: Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.
- Benefits: Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.
Hip-In Steps
- Movement: Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.
- Target Muscles: Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.
- Benefits: Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.
Key Benefits of Lateral Steps
| Benefit | Description |
|---|---|
| Strengthening Hip Abductors | Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. |
| Enhancing Stability | Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. |
| Improving Coordination | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |
Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.
name: Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

description:
Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.
Overview
Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.
Benefits
- Improves balance: Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.
- Enhances proprioception: Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.
- Supports rehabilitation: Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.
How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
Steps
1. Preparation: Stand on a stable surface or a box.
2. Takeoff: Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.
3. Landing: Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.
4. Hold position: Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.
5. Reset: Return to the starting position and repeat.
Key Points to Remember
- Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.
- Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.
- Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.
Conclusion
Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.
name: Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

description:
Step into the V-squat machine facing the pad, the opposite way from the regular V-squat, so that your chest rests against the pad and your shoulders sit under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform about shoulder width apart and release the safety.
Brace your core and lower yourself by bending your knees and pushing the hips back until your thighs are roughly parallel to the platform. Drive back up through the heels without locking out the knees.
Compared to the regular V-squat, the reversed position shifts the emphasis towards the glutes and hamstrings.
name: Reverse V-Squat

description: Pike push-up with legs on an elevated surface. Progression to handstand push-up.
name: Box Handstand Push-up

description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet about hip-width apart, holding one end in each hand in front of your thighs. Keeping your arms straight with a slight bend in the elbows, raise your hands forward to shoulder height, then lower slowly under control. Can be done with both arms together or alternating. Use a heavier band or shorten the band to increase resistance.
name: Banded Front Raise

description: Sit at a plate-loaded (lever) lat pulldown machine with your thighs secured under the pads. Grip the handles overhead with arms fully extended. Pull the handles down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, squeezing your lats at the bottom. Return slowly to full extension. Resistance comes from weight plates loaded on the machine's lever arms rather than a cable stack.
name: Plate-Loaded Lat Pulldown

description: Set a cable pulley at the lowest position and attach a single handle. Stand side-on to the machine, hold the frame with your near hand and lean your body away so you hang at an angle. With the far hand, grasp the handle in front of your hips and raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower slowly. The lean increases tension on the side delts at the bottom of the movement. Complete all reps, then switch sides.
name: Lean-Away Cable Lateral Raise

description:
Adjust the seat so that your armpits rest on the top edge of the pad and your upper arms lie flat on it. Grip the handles with your palms facing up.
Curl the handles up by bending your elbows, without lifting your upper arms off the pad or leaning back. Squeeze the biceps briefly at the top, then lower the handles slowly until your arms are almost straight.
name: Preacher Curl Machine

description: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.
name: Seated Band Row

description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.
name: FlexBar Wrist Extension

description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing up and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist extend back, then curl the wrist up to raise the bar while the forearm stays still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. Works the wrist flexors, and is the companion movement to FlexBar wrist extension for balanced forearm strengthening.
name: FlexBar Wrist Flexion

description: An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.
name: FlexBar Tyler Twist

name: Squat -> Stand Coordination

description:
Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit comfortably. Breathe in slowly into your belly and let your pelvic floor relax and gently lengthen downwards, without pushing or straining. Breathe out and let the pelvic floor return to its resting position. Repeat slowly for several breaths.
The reverse Kegel trains relaxing the pelvic floor, the opposite of the contraction in a regular Kegel exercise.
name: Gentle Reverse Kegels

description:
Lie on your back and pull your knees towards your armpits. Hold the outside of your feet, your ankles or your shins, with the soles of your feet facing the ceiling and your shins roughly vertical.
Gently pull your feet down to open the hips while keeping your lower back and head on the floor. Hold the position and breathe calmly, you can also rock gently from side to side.
name: Happy Baby

description:
Stand upright with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging at your sides and feet hip-width apart. For a larger range of motion, stand with the balls of your feet on a step or a weight plate.
Rise up onto your toes as high as you can and pause briefly at the top. Then lower your heels slowly until you feel a stretch in your calves. Keep your knees straight but not locked and your upper body upright.
name: Dumbbell Calf Raise

description: Use the same technic as your normal squat. Except that you make a pause at the bottom of the squat for about 1-2 seconds, in other words a bit longer than your normal squat.
name: Paused Squats

description:
Go into a one-legged kneeling position and grab the cable from the lowest position.
Rotate the upper torso to get into the starting position and bend the upper torso a little bit sidewise.
Place the unused hand on the knee.
Pull the cable while rotating the upper torso.
name: Single-Arm Cable Row with Rotation (Floor)

description: A gentle stretch to restore full knee extension. Sit with one leg stretched out in front of you and the heel propped on the floor or a low surface, so the knee is unsupported. Place both hands on the thigh just above the kneecap. Keeping the leg relaxed, gently press down through the hands toward the floor until you feel a stretch behind the knee, and hold for about three seconds before releasing. The pressure should produce a stretch, never sharp pain. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch legs.
name: Seated Knee Extension with Overpressure

description: A banded walking drill for the glutes and hip stabilisers. Place a mini band around both thighs just above the knees, or around the ankles for a harder version. Stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is under tension, then sink into a quarter-squat with the chest up. Walk forward with small diagonal steps, pushing each leg out against the band and keeping the knees tracking over the toes rather than letting them fall inward. Walk forward for the prescribed number of steps, then walk backward to return, keeping the band under tension throughout.
name: Banded Monster Walk

description: Stand on a step or a sturdy raised surface with the balls of both feet on the edge and the heels hanging off, holding a rail or wall for balance. Let one or both heels drop below the level of the step until you feel a stretch through the calf, and hold. Keep the knee straight to stretch the gastrocnemius, or bend the knee slightly to bias the soleus lower down. Hold for the prescribed time, typically 30 seconds, without bouncing, then switch sides if stretching one leg at a time.
name: Step Calf Stretch

description: A balance and proprioception drill. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and the other foot lifted clear of the floor, then close your eyes and hold the position. Without visual feedback the ankle and hip stabilisers have to do the work, so expect noticeable wobble. Stand within reach of a wall, counter or chair so you can steady yourself if needed. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch legs. Commonly prescribed in rehabilitation after ankle or knee injury.
name: Single-Leg Balance with Eyes Closed

aliases: Kettlebell Body Circle on One Leg
description: A balance drill that adds a moving load. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, holding a kettlebell in one hand. Pass the kettlebell around your body in a circle, handing it from one hand to the other in front and behind you, while keeping your balance on the standing leg. Keep the hips level and the torso upright; the shifting weight of the bell constantly changes your centre of mass, which is what trains the hip and ankle stabilisers. Complete the prescribed number of circles, reverse direction, then switch legs. Use a light bell to start.
name: Single-Leg Balance with Kettlebell Circles

description:
How to Perform It
- Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral or overhand grip.
- Hinge at the hips, pushing your glutes back, until your torso is roughly 45–75 degrees to the floor. Keep a slight bend in your knees.
- Let the dumbbells hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.
- Keep your back flat, chest up, and core braced — avoid rounding your spine.
- Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage/hips, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.
- Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
- Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.
- Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Key Coaching Cues
- Hinge from the hips, not the lower back
- Keep the spine neutral throughout — no rounding
- Lead with the elbows, not the hands
- Avoid using momentum or jerking the weight up
- Control the eccentric (lowering) phase rather than letting the weights drop
name: Bent Over Dumbbell Rows (Two Arms)

description: 1m30s of walking (~4.5 km/h) to 30 s of jog (7 km/h) and repeat
name: Alternate Walking

description:
Video can be found here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGPBSqxKGAc
Full-body mobility and dynamic warm-up routine (3–5 minutes) to prepare joints, muscles, and the cardiovascular system for workout.
Movement Flow:
Deep Breathing & Arm Raises: Inhale while raising arms laterally overhead, exhale as you lower them.
Knee Bends: Soft, rhythmic knee flexions synchronized with arm swings.
Arm Circles: Large full-range arm rotations forward, then backward to open up the chest and shoulder girdle.
Chest Expansion: Cross arms in front of the chest and open wide to the sides.
Side Bends: Reach overhead to stretch the lateral torso left and right with a smooth side flexion.
Forward & Back Bends: Gently hinge at the hips to reach forward, then return upright with a mild spinal extension.
Torso Twists: Swing arms side-to-side to rotate the spine and loosen the core.
Ankle Mobility / Light Bounces: Soft heel lifts or light bouncing on toes to warm up lower leg joints and tendons.
name: Radio Taiso

description:
Kelso shrugs are a variation of scapular shrugs designed primarily to train scapular retraction, with particular emphasis on the middle trapezius, rhomboids, and, secondarily, the lower trapezius. Unlike conventional shrugs, the goal is not to elevate the shoulders toward the ears, but rather to pull the shoulder blades backward.
They are typically performed with the chest supported on an incline bench, using either dumbbells or a barbell:
1. Lie face down on an incline bench, with your arms extended toward the floor.
2. Keep your elbows almost completely locked throughout the movement.
3. Starting with the shoulder blades slightly protracted, retract them, trying to bring them closer together.
4. Keep your chest firmly supported on the bench; avoid turning the movement into a row by extending your torso.
5. Briefly hold the fully retracted position, then return in a controlled manner, allowing the shoulder blades to separate.
name: Kelso Shrugs

description:
1. Starting position: Lie flat on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor (or stand/sit upright).
2. Exhalation: Fully exhale all the air from your lungs through your mouth.
3. Contraction: Draw your navel in towards your spine as far as possible, pulling your stomach inward and up under your ribcage.
4. Hold: Hold this isometric contraction without breathing for 10 to 20 seconds.
5. Release: Slowly inhale through your nose to release the tension and relax your abdominals.
6. Repeat: Rest briefly and perform the desired number of sets.
name: Stomach Vacuum

description:
Starting position
Step into the captain's chair (vertical knee raise station). Rest your forearms on the pads and hold the handles. Keep your upper body upright, look straight ahead and press your back against the pad, without rounding or arching it. Your legs are almost straight with a slight bend in the knees, your feet are off the floor and your legs are together.
Movement
Pull your bent legs up, bringing your knees towards your chest. Only go as high as you can while keeping good form, with your legs together the whole time. Then lower your legs again while inhaling, without putting your feet back on the floor.
name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise

description:
Starting position
Step into the captain's chair (dip station). Rest your forearms on the pads and grip the handles firmly. Keep your back upright and close to the pad and look straight ahead. Bend your legs so that your thighs and shins form roughly a right angle.
Movement
Raise your knees while turning your legs slightly to one side, about 30-45 degrees, keeping your thighs parallel to the floor. Then do the same to the other side. You can pause briefly in the middle or go straight to the other side.
name: Captain's Chair Oblique Knee Raise

description: Weighted neck flexion is an isolation exercise designed to strengthen the anterior (front) neck flexor muscles by bringing your chin toward your chest against external resistance (most commonly a light weight plate, resistance band, or neck harness).
name: Weighted neck flexion

description: Strength training exercise where you push a weight away from your body using one leg at a time on a leg press machine. It helps to improve leg strength, balance, and muscular symmetry by isolating each leg individually. This exercise is particularly useful for identifying and correcting muscle imbalances between your legs.
name: Single leg press

description: Perform a row using gymnastic rings, but with the body position somewhere between vertical and horizontal. Go closer to horizontal to make it harder.
name: Incline Row - Rings

description:
Starting Position
• Feet: Place the soles of your feet flat against a vertical wall, with your toes or balls of your feet on the floor.
• Hands: Position your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart, directly under your lower chest or solar plexus.
• Body: Keep your core tight, glutes squeezed, and head in a neutral position. Your knees should hover a few inches above the floor without touching it.
Movement Pattern
1. Lower Down: Flex your elbows (tucked around 45 degrees) to lower your chest toward the floor, stopping just a few centimeters short of touching the ground.
2. Rock Back: As you press upward through your arms, push your hips backward and bend your knees, rocking your weight toward your heels while keeping your shins nearly parallel to the floor.
3. Drive Forward: Explode forward from your lower-body/crouched position, shifting your weight back into the starting push-up plank stance to complete the repetition.
Key Tips for Proper Form
• Keep Knees Low: Do not let your knees or hips pike high up in the air; keep the motion low and horizontal.
• Maintain Wall Contact: Keep the soles of your feet pressed against the wall so you don't lose your leverage.
• Engage the Core: Avoid arching your lower back by tilting your pelvis backward and bracing your abs.
name: Tyson push-ups

description: Start on all fours with your palms flat on the floor. Slowly rock forward and backward, keeping your hands planted. Move only within a comfortable, pain-free wrist range to gently improve mobility and flexibility.
name: Wrist rocks

description: Start in a straight-arm plank with your hands under your shoulders. Keep your elbows locked and move only your shoulder blades: let your chest sink slightly, then push the floor away to spread the shoulder blades. Move in a comfortable, controlled range.
name: Scapular Pushups

description: Dumbbell squats with elevated heel position. Stand on either squat wedges or weight plates to raise heels higher than toes, while holding the dumbbells on your sides.
name: Dumbbell cyclist squat

description:
Push ups for targeting triceps.
- Start with a plank position with your hands directly below your shoulders, feet together.
- When descending, keep your elbows pinned to your sides. Upper arms straight back.
- Lower until your chest touches the floor, then return.
name: Triceps push up

description: Extend your right arm straight across your chest toward the left. Hook your left arm around your right elbow and pull your right arm a little closer to your body. Keep your shoulder down as you do this. Repeat on the other side.
name: Cross-Body Stretch

description: Extend your right arm straight out in front of you, with your palm facing up (fingers pointing toward the floor). Using your left hand, gently pull the fingers of your right hand toward you until you feel a stretch in your forearm and biceps.
name: Wrist Stretch

description: Stand on one leg (hold onto a wall if necessary). Use your hand to grasp the ankle of your other leg and gently pull your heel toward your buttocks. Make sure your knees stay close together and that you push your pelvis slightly forward (avoid arching your back).
name: Quadriceps Stretch

description:
One of the best exercises for the rectus abdominis muscles. Lie on your back with your legs straight and your arms close to your sides. Lift your head off the floor and raise your legs and arms about 15 centimeters off the floor. Your palms should face down, and look up at the ceiling.
Now bend your legs and at the same time sit up so that your knees and chest almost touch. Only your buttocks are still on the floor. Your arms are now extended at shoulder height. Then slowly return to the starting position with your arms and legs extended and your head raised.
name: V-Up

description: A static hold from a pull-up bar with straight elbows and actively depressed, stabilized shoulders. Grip a secure bar and let your body hang under control. Keep your elbows straight and gently draw your shoulders down, away from your ears. Maintain this active shoulder position without pulling up, swinging, or repeatedly moving the shoulder blades. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier if your grip opens, shoulder control deteriorates, or pain occurs. Record actual seconds, grip, and any assistance used. This is distinct from a relaxed passive dead hang or a moving scapular pull-up.
name: Active Hang

description: A static bodyweight support with both hands and feet on the floor and hips raised in a pike position. Place your hands and feet securely on the floor, then raise your hips. Keep your elbows straight and actively push the floor away through your shoulders. Maintain a controlled, stationary position without bending your elbows, lowering your head for push-up repetitions, or raising your feet onto a surface. Hold for up to 30 seconds. Stop earlier for loss of alignment, loss of active shoulder support, or pain. Record actual seconds, hand and foot spacing, and alignment. This is the floor variation, not a pike push-up or an elevated-feet pike hold.
name: Pike Hold (Floor)

description: Swim one short pool length at a gentle pace while focusing on a relaxed body position and a steady exhale into the water between breaths. Pause at the wall between lengths. This is a moving swim technique drill, not stationary bobbing or a kickboard-only exercise.
name: Exhale and Body-position Swim Drill

description: Place both hands against a wall above shoulder height. Step back and gently move the chest downward while reaching the arms overhead, keeping the back controlled. Hold a comfortable shoulder flexion stretch without forcing the range or arching the lower back.
name: Shoulder Flexion Wall Stretch

description: Hold a stable straight bar in front of the hips with both arms straight. Keep both feet on the floor or a stable platform so they assist your body weight. Maintain steady shoulders and a controlled supported position without swinging. This is a feet-assisted straight-bar support hold, not a ring hold or a full dip.
name: Feet-assisted Straight-bar Support

description: Swim a short pool length at a controlled brisk effort, maintaining smooth strokes and steady breathing. Stop at the wall for the prescribed recovery before the next repeat. This is a submaximal swim interval, not an all-out sprint; distance, repeats and rest are set by the routine.
name: Controlled Brisk Swim

description: Hold a stable support in front of you and lower into a comfortable deep squat with both feet grounded. Use the support for balance and to control depth. Maintain the squat hold without bouncing or forcing the hips or ankles farther than a comfortable range.

description: Stand tall with your arm hanging straight down by your side. Hold a dumbbell by one end of the handle so the weighted end points forward and your thumb is on top. Keep the arm completely still and tip the weighted end up toward the ceiling using only the wrist, then lower it slowly. This trains radial deviation, the riser used in arm wrestling. Slide your hand further from the weight to make it harder.
name: Dumbbell Wrist Rising

description: Set up exactly as for dumbbell wrist rising: arm straight down by your side, dumbbell held at one end with the weight pointing forward. Tip the weight up to the top position and hold it still for the set time without letting it drop. This builds tendon strength in the riser for arm wrestling. Start light and stop if you feel sharp pain in the wrist or elbow.
name: Isometric Wrist Rising Hold

description: Rest your forearm on a bench or your knee and hold a light kettlebell by the handle with the bell hanging down. Keeping the elbow and forearm still, slowly rotate your wrist so the palm turns down, then rotate back so the palm turns up. Do the set number of turns in each direction. This trains pronation and supination for grip and arm wrestling.
name: Kettlebell Wrist Turnover

description: Rest your forearm on a bench with the palm facing in and the thumb on top. Hold a dumbbell by one end with the weighted end pointing up. Let the weight tip about 45 degrees toward the palm up side, then stop it and hold that position for the set time. The muscles that stop it falling are your pronators, which roll the hand over in arm wrestling. Start with a light weight because the leverage is high.
name: Isometric Dumbbell Pronation Hold

description: Sit on a bench with your forearm resting on your thigh, palm facing up, holding a dumbbell or barbell. Curl the wrist all the way up and hold the top position for the set time, squeezing hard. This builds cupping strength and tendon resilience for grip and arm wrestling. Do it straight after your wrist curls without changing seats.
name: Isometric Wrist Curl Hold

description: Stand on a box or bench under a pull-up bar and step up so your chin is above the bar with your elbows fully bent. Take your feet off the box and lower yourself as slowly as you can, aiming for five seconds, until your arms are straight. Step back onto the box and repeat. This builds the strength needed for full pull-ups.
name: Slow Eccentric Pull-Up Negative

description: Use a box or bench to get your chin above a pull-up bar with your elbows fully bent and shoulders pulled down. Take your feet off the box and hold that top position still for the set time. Keep your chest up and do not let your chin drop below the bar. This strengthens the hardest part of the pull-up.
name: Pull-Up Top Position Hold

description: Hang two towels over a pull-up bar, one for each hand. Grip a towel tightly in each hand and hang with your arms straight and your shoulders active for as long as you can. The thick, unstable towels make your grip work much harder than a normal bar. This builds crushing grip strength for arm wrestling.
name: Towel Grip Dead Hang

description: Attach a single handle to a low cable. Rest your forearm on a bench or your thigh with the palm facing up and the cable pulling your hand away from you. Curl your fingers and wrist toward you as if cupping a ball, squeeze for a second, then lower slowly. This builds the wrist flexion used to control an opponent's hand in arm wrestling.
name: Cable Cupping

description: Set a cable at chest height and stand side on, holding the handle with your elbow bent about ninety degrees in front of you, like an arm wrestling setup. Pull the handle toward your body using your biceps and back, keeping the wrist cupped, then return slowly. This trains the hook or back pressure used in arm wrestling.
name: Cable Back Pressure

description: Set a cable at chest height and stand side on with the cable on your working side. Hold the handle with your elbow bent about ninety degrees and close to your body. Press the handle across your body toward your opposite side using your chest and shoulder, then return slowly. This trains the side pressure used to pin an opponent in arm wrestling.
name: Cable Side Pressure

description: Attach a strap or handle to a cable at hand height so the cable pulls your palm toward facing up. Keep your elbow bent at your side and still. Rotate your forearm so the palm turns down against the cable, then let it rotate back slowly. This builds pronation strength for rolling an opponent's hand in arm wrestling.
name: Cable Wrist Pronation

description: Attach a strap or handle to a cable at hand height so the cable pulls your palm toward facing down. Keep your elbow bent at your side and still. Rotate your forearm so the palm turns up against the cable, then let it rotate back slowly. This balances pronation work and protects the elbow.
name: Cable Wrist Supination

description: Hold a sledgehammer or an empty dumbbell handle with a plate on one end near the bottom of the handle, arm by your side. Using only the wrist, lift the head up in front of you, then lower it slowly. Turn around so the head is behind you to train the opposite direction. Move your hand further from the weight to make it harder.
name: Hammer Levering

description: Stand with your arm straight down by your side. Hold a dumbbell by one end of the handle with the weighted end pointing behind you. Keeping the arm still, lift the weighted end up behind you using only the wrist, then lower it slowly. This is the opposite of wrist rising and keeps the wrist balanced.
name: Dumbbell Ulnar Deviation

description: Hold a wrist roller, a short bar with a rope and a small weight attached, with both hands at shoulder height and arms straight out in front. Roll the bar with your wrists to wind the rope up until the weight reaches the bar, then unwind it slowly. Roll forward and backward on different sets to train both sides of the forearm.
name: Wrist Roller

description: Hold a spring hand gripper deep in your palm. Squeeze until the handles touch, hold for a second, then open slowly. Use a gripper strength you can close for the target reps. This builds crushing grip strength for holding on in arm wrestling and in pulling exercises.
name: Hand Gripper Squeeze

description: Put a small rubber band around all five fingertips. Spread your fingers and thumb open as wide as possible against the band, hold for a second, then close slowly. This trains the extensor muscles that open the hand and balances heavy gripping, which helps keep the elbows and wrists healthy.
name: Band Finger Extensions

description: Place a weight plate on the floor with the hub facing up, or use a loading pin with a plate attached. Pinch the hub with your fingertips on one side and your thumb on the other, then stand up and hold it for the set time. This builds thumb and pinch strength, which helps grip control in arm wrestling.
name: Hub Lift

description: Fit thick grip sleeves over two dumbbell handles, or wrap the handles in a towel to make them thicker. Stand tall holding one in each hand at your sides and hold for the set time without letting the handles roll in your hands. The thicker handle makes your fingers and thumb work much harder than a normal grip.
name: Fat Grip Dumbbell Hold

description: Fill a deep bucket with dry rice. Push your hand into the rice and repeatedly open and close your fist, twist your wrist both ways, and spread your fingers against the rice for the set time. This is a low impact way to train every muscle of the hand and forearm and is good for warming up or recovery.
name: Rice Bucket Training

description: Hang two towels over a pull-up bar and grip one in each hand. Pull yourself up until your hands are near your chin, then lower slowly to straight arms. Holding the towels makes your grip work much harder than a normal pull-up. Use assistance or do negatives if you cannot do full reps yet.
name: Towel Pull-Up

description: Grip a hanging climbing rope with both hands overhead. Pull yourself up hand over hand, using your legs to clamp the rope if needed, then climb down with control. Beginners can start seated on the floor and pull up to standing. This builds pulling and grip strength together.
name: Rope Climb

description: Stand under a pull-up bar on the floor or a low box so you can reach the bar with bent arms. Jump and pull at the same time until your chin passes the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can. This is a beginner step toward full pull-ups.
name: Jumping Pull-Up

description: Perform the leg press with controlled form, feet shoulder-width on the platform, lower slowly without letting the pelvis lift, keep knees tracking over toes, breathe steadily.
name: Leg Press (Custom)

description: Perform the Bulgarian split squat with an upright torso, rear foot on a bench, lower until the front thigh is parallel, keep the knee over the toes, hold a rack for balance if needed.
name: Bulgarian Split Squat (Custom)

description: Perform the hip thrust with shoulder blades on the bench, drive through the heels, squeeze the glutes at the top for one second, avoid overextending the lower back, lower slowly.
name: Hip Thrust (Custom)

description: Lie on your back, press your lower back into the floor, extend opposite arm and leg slowly, keep the spine neutral, breathe steadily, return under control without arching.
name: Dead Bug (Custom)

description: On all fours, extend opposite arm and leg, keep the pelvis level and the spine neutral, move slowly under control, return to the start without letting the lower back sag.
name: Bird Dog (Custom)

description: Hold a side plank on your elbow, keep pelvis, ribcage and spine aligned in one straight line, breathe normally, avoid sagging the hips or shrugging the shoulder.
name: Side Plank (Custom)

description: Sit with your back supported, keep the upper arms fixed at your sides, curl the dumbbells up, pause briefly at the top, lower slowly under control without swinging the back.
name: Seated Dumbbell Biceps Curl (Custom)

description: Hang from the rings, tuck the pelvis first, then raise the legs and lift the hips, keep the torso still without swinging, lower slowly under control, breathe steadily.
name: Hanging Leg Raise with Hip Lift on Rings (Custom)

description: Stand and side-bend slowly to one side, feel a gentle stretch along the waist, hold for thirty seconds, switch sides, move gently and stop if you feel sharp pain.
name: Quadratus Lumborum Stretch (Custom)

description: Stand and lift one bent knee out to the side with external rotation, move slowly under control, ten reps per side, hold a wall for balance if needed, keep the torso upright.
name: Standing Leg Lift with External Rotation (Custom)

description: Lie face down with legs straight, kick both legs back, squeeze the glutes, keep the lower back flat, move slowly under control, ten reps per set, breathe steadily.
name: Prone Leg Kickback (Custom)

description: Lie on your back, breathe in fully, let the ribs sink down, press the lower back into the floor, exhale slowly while keeping intra-abdominal pressure, five reps per set.
name: Dead Bug Breathing (Custom)

description: Lie on your back with both legs extended. Raise one leg straight up and gently pull it towards your upper body with both hands around your thigh. Keep the knee as straight as possible and your lower back on the mat. Hold the stretch, then switch legs.
name: Straight Leg Hamstring Stretch
